chapter_theme: Under the heading முயற்சி, thirteen verses on effort: one is one's own physician and no helper does one's work, the doer outranks the learned and the old, neither the smallness of a task nor the lack of kin excuses sloth, action must be weighed and done by means that succeed, delegation from sloth and dependence on kings fail, and folded hands before fate end no trouble.

149.reading: The verse says one need not go looking for helpers in the thought that one needs them, since no one does for another what that other must do, and closes that each is his own physician.
149.nuance: Line 3 is a rhetorical question answered at once (உண்டோ மற்றில்லை), so the denial is absolute: the verse does not say helpers are bad, only that the striver's own task cannot be carried by them.

pazhamozhi.literal: each person is his own physician

story.act: no story; the physician image is applied to anyone who waits on helpers

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one's own effort, not a sought-out helper, cures one's own need

150.reading: The verse calls wise the man who carries a task through to its end even if he has learned nothing, and closes that the man who acts, though young, is the elder.
150.nuance: The verse detaches அறிவு from கல்வி: wisdom is shown in finishing the work (அற்ற முடிப்போன்), and the proverb moves seniority likewise from years to deeds. The address to the lord of the shore (நீத்தநீர்ச் சேர்ப்ப) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: the man who does the work is the elder even if he is young

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: rank in wisdom goes to the one who completes the task, not to learning or age

151.reading: The verse names the strivers as those who do வேளாண்மை, tend guests, are strong with the sword in fierce battle and have none of the sloth that drags down effort, and closes that the life of those who do not toil never comes right.
151.nuance: வேளாண்மை beside விருந்தோம்பி is most likely beneficence to guests rather than farming, as in the old pairing of the two words; the verse then joins household giving and battle valour under one demand for toil (தாளாண்மை).

pazhamozhi.literal: the life of those who do not labour does not become well ordered

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: household giving and valour alike need unremitting effort

152.reading: The verse says that one who sits idle reasoning that a single small effort helps nothing incurs a great fault, and that those who do not stir cannot get through even that very day.
152.nuance: The quotation marks enclose only சென்றது பேரா தவர், which is not a whole saying; the proverb probably includes அன்றைப் பகலேயும் வாழ்கலார் and perhaps நின்றது. நின்றது சென்றது may mean 'what remains and what has gone' or 'whether it stays or goes'; the reading takes பேராதவர் as those who do not move.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who do not stir (from what has gone)

story.act: no story; applied to the idler who scorns small effort

pazhamozhi.applied_to: neglecting small efforts as useless leaves one unable to live even a day

153.reading: The verse says no one should sink into sloth saying 'I have no one dear, who else is mine, I am alone', but should strive without weariness, and closes that those without weariness never fail to reach what they set out for.
153.nuance: முனிவு here is weariness or vexation with the task; the verse turns the lack of kin, usually a reason for pity, into a mere excuse for sloth.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those without weariness there is no failing to reach what they intended

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the friendless man's own unwearied effort is enough to reach his aim

154.reading: The verse says the clever take up a matter after weighing themselves, weighing their helpers and weighing the gain, and that otherwise, if one does anything with anything, it turns into anything at all.
154.nuance: The repeated யாதானும் makes the proverb enact its point: random means and random action give a random result.

pazhamozhi.proverb: யாதானும் ஒன்றுகொண்டு யாதானும் செய்தக்கால் யாதானும் ஆகி விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: if you take up anything and do anything, it becomes anything

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: action without weighing self, helpers and gain has no determinate outcome

155.reading: Since the wrath of the broad-shouldered Chola destroyed even the fort that hung in the sky, the verse bids one strive by means that will succeed, and closes that when a sharp arrow is drawn to its base no fortress holds.
155.nuance: The heroic memory is used for method, not for praise: what brought the sky-fort down was force applied by the right means (முடியும் திறத்தால்), and the arrow drawn full to the head is that means in small.
155.domain_note: a king or warrior attacking a stronghold

pazhamozhi.literal: if the sharp arrow is drawn back to its base there is no defence against it

story.act: the Chola whose wrath destroyed the fort hanging in the sky
story.tradition: by tradition the Chola known as destroyer of the hanging fort (தூங்கெயில்); the verse names him only as செம்பியன்

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort applied by an effective method overcomes any obstacle

156.reading: The verse says no one should bring about his own ruin by saying 'there is nothing in me, I have no kin', and closes that for those whose forearms are long the shoulders are everywhere well rounded and very great.
156.nuance: The proverb puts strength in one's own body: long arms go with great shoulders, so reach and power belong to the person, not to his kin. எங்காணும் நன்கு திரண்டு is taken with the shoulders; the link of the proverb to effort is implied, not stated.

pazhamozhi.literal: those with long forearms have very great shoulders

story.act: no story; the bodily sign of the strong man is applied to anyone who pleads lack of kin

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one's own capacity, not wealth or kin, is the ground of strength

157.reading: The verse says that those who, seeking great wealth beyond their land, attach themselves to the good among worthy kings but find no firm footing on the ground, are called by those who see them 'a crow on a pestle'.
157.nuance: A crow perched on a pestle in use must fly up at every stroke; the verse's நிலத்து நிலைகொள்ளாக் காலர் may mean the courtiers' own unsteadiness or the instability of any footing gained through a king's favour. Its place under முயற்சி suggests the contrast with wealth won by one's own effort.
157.domain_note: those who seek wealth in a king's service

story.act: no story; applied to the hanger-on at court

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth sought through attachment to kings gives no stable place

158.reading: The verse says that if men take up their own task as foremost, then out of sloth put it in the hands of those with no firm grip, and themselves drop their grip and wander off, the task will show itself greatly spilled and run to waste.
158.nuance: கடைப்பிடி is said twice, of the deputies who lack it and of the master who lets it go; the failure is double, in the choice of hands and in one's own slackening.

pazhamozhi.literal: it will show itself greatly spilled and running away

story.act: no story; applied to the master who delegates and wanders

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a task handed to the irresolute through sloth comes to ruin

159.reading: The verse says it is no use for those who will not do with their own effort what they can do to wait, thinking they will have it done later by another, for, lord of the hill land of red-water falls, would those who will not even heat water leap into fire?
159.nuance: The proverb reads most naturally of the hoped-for helper: one who will not do even a small easy service for you will not do a hard one. It could also be read of the idler himself, who will not do the great thing if he will not do the small.

pazhamozhi.literal: would those who will not even heat water leap into fire?

story.act: no story; applied to the man who waits for another to do his work

pazhamozhi.applied_to: others will not do the hard part of one's task when they will not do the easy part

160.reading: The verse asks whether suffering ends by sitting with folded hands, saying 'He apportioned everything beforehand', and closes that when the leaf written earlier is faulty there is nothing the one who smears it over cannot make.
160.nuance: The writer of the leaf is the one who fixed fate (முழுதுடன் முன்னே வகுத்தவன்). இழுகினான் is taken as one who smears out and rewrites the palm leaf, so effort can correct a bad fate; if it is read as 'the slack man', the proverb instead says the leaf does not fail the idler, with a reversed sense.

pazhamozhi.proverb: இழுகினான் ஆகாப்ப தில்லையே முன்னம் எழுதினான் ஓலை பழுது
pazhamozhi.literal: if the leaf written before is faulty, nothing is beyond the one who smears it over

story.act: no story; the scribe's correction of a palm leaf is applied to fate

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort can rewrite what fate wrote, so passive worship of the fixer of fate ends no trouble

161.reading: The verse says there is no effort for what is done, no increase for what broke off unfinished, no hardship for one who is thoroughly capable, and closes that in the world there is no name for what does not exist.
161.nuance: The four clauses share the frame X-க்கு இல்லை Y, so the proverb reads as the last of a series: what was never done earns no name. வடிந்தற வல்லதற்கு is of doubtful sense; taken here as one refined to full capacity.

pazhamozhi.literal: in the world there is no name for what does not exist

story.act: no story; the general truth closes a series of four

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an undone or half-done work gets no renown

links.note: Kural 442 bids one cherish as support those who remove an affliction that has come and guard against one to come; Pazhamozhi 149 says one need not seek helpers at all, since each is his own physician.
links.teaches: The Kural's helper is a physician to the king, and Pazhamozhi takes the same healing image back for the self, so the two disagree on whether one's trouble can be cured from outside.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's healer into the striver himself, denying that another can do one's own work.

links.note: Kural 410 sets the unlearned to the learned as beasts to men; Pazhamozhi 150 calls wise the man who finishes his task even if he has learned nothing.
links.teaches: Read together, the two give rival measures of a person: the Kural ranks by what one has studied, Pazhamozhi by what one has completed, and on its reading the unlearned doer outranks the idle learned.
links.list_adds: its proverb moves rank from learning and age to finished work, a criterion the couplet does not admit.

links.note: Kural 81 says household life exists for tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை); Pazhamozhi 151 uses the same pair of words and sets battle valour and freedom from sloth beside them.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's purpose of the household needs a means it does not name: hospitality is sustained only by toil, so giving to guests stands with valour as a fruit of effort.
links.list_adds: it puts hospitality, beneficence and sword-valour in one series closed by toil, making giving an outcome of effort rather than the end of the household alone.

links.note: Kural 611 forbids slackening because a task seems hard; Pazhamozhi 152 forbids it because a single effort seems too small to help.
links.teaches: Together they close both exits from effort: the Kural answers the excuse that the task is too great, Pazhamozhi the excuse that one's part is too small.
links.list_adds: it names the opposite excuse to the couplet's and gives the cost, not surviving even the day.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 153 promises that the unwearied never fail to reach their aim; Naladiyar 194 makes manliness standing firm even when the thing does not succeed.
links.teaches: The pair splits the reward of effort: Pazhamozhi gives the friendless striver success as his warrant, while the Naladiyar holds that persistence is the measure even when success does not come.
links.list_adds: it ties effort to the excuse of having no kin and guarantees success, where the quatrain detaches manliness from success.

links.note: Kural 471 bids one weigh the strength of the deed, one's own, the opponent's and the allies' before acting; Pazhamozhi 154 weighs oneself, one's helpers and the gain, using the same verb தூக்கி.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi adds the gain to the Kural's weighing of strengths and says what follows without it, so the reckoning is shown to be of purpose as well as of power.
links.list_adds: it replaces the enemy's strength with the gain in the reckoning and adds, through its proverb, the formless result of unweighed action.

links.note: Purananuru 39 tells a Chola that, with ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort, killing is not his own fame; Pazhamozhi 155 recalls the same Chola feat of the fort in the sky.
links.teaches: The puram poem treats the hanging fort as inherited glory a descendant cannot claim, while the ethics verse turns it into a lesson anyone can use: the fort fell to force applied by the right means.

links.note: Both verses forbid pleading 'I have no kin' as a reason to fail; 153 answers it with unwearied effort, 156 with the image of the long-armed man's great shoulders.
links.teaches: The pair shows the heading's single counsel argued two ways, by the promise of success and by the sign of strength in one's own body, so the lack of kin is answered both by outcome and by capacity.

links.note: Kural 691 tells those who attach themselves to kings to stay like fire-warmers, neither far nor near; Pazhamozhi 157 calls those who seek wealth through kings a crow on a pestle.
links.teaches: The Kural offers a way to keep a safe place by the king, and Pazhamozhi doubts that such a place can be kept: the courtier's perch moves with every stroke.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes court dependence itself unstable and sets it against wealth won by effort, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Kural 517 says to examine who will finish a task by what means and then leave it to him; Pazhamozhi 158 shows the task handed out of sloth to those without firm grip, while the master too lets go.
links.teaches: The Kural's letting go is safe only after examination; Pazhamozhi shows the same handing-over done from sloth, so delegation is a virtue or a ruin depending on why it is done.
links.list_adds: it names the motive, sloth, and the double loss of grip, which the couplet's rule of choosing assumes away.

links.note: 149 says no one does for another what that other must do; 159 applies it to the man who waits to have his task done later by someone else.
links.teaches: 159 supplies the evidence for 149's flat denial: the helper one waits for will not even heat water, so he will not leap into fire for one.

links.note: Naladiyar 110 says what was set in the early mark neither shrinks nor grows and comes as due; Pazhamozhi 160, on the reading that the smearer rewrites the leaf, says a faulty written fate can be remade.
links.teaches: The two give opposite answers to what one should do before a fixed fate: the Naladiyar counsels calm acceptance, Pazhamozhi effort that rewrites the leaf, and both reject grieving or idle worship.
links.list_adds: its proverb casts fate as a palm-leaf document that a later hand can correct, against the quatrain's mark that cannot change.

links.note: Kural 620 says those who toil without flagging see even fate's back; Pazhamozhi 160 says folded hands before the one who fixed fate end no trouble.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi names the rival of effort that the Kural leaves unstated, pious resignation, and replaces the Kural's battle image with a scribe correcting a leaf.
links.list_adds: it sets worship of the fixer of fate against effort, making resignation itself the error.

links.note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die midway, since the world's regard follows how one deals with unfinished work; Pazhamozhi 161 says what broke off unfinished has no increase and what does not exist has no name.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi states as a law of naming what the Kural states as social regard: the half-done work does not earn a poor name but no name at all.
links.list_adds: its four parallel clauses rank the finished, the broken-off and the capable, ending in the proverb that the undone has no name.

source_issues: 152 line 4: the quotation marks enclose only சென்றது பேரா தவர், which is not a complete saying; the proverb probably begins earlier in line 3.
159 line 3: the proverb opens with a quotation mark ('பாய்பவோ) that is never closed.
160 line 3-4: இழுகினான் ஆகாப்ப தில்லையே is obscure, and the proverb's sense reverses with the reading of இழுகினான்.
161 line 2: வடிந்தற வல்லதற்கு is of doubtful sense.
